Obscure
ŏb-skūr´
adj. (dark; without light)
From the Latin obscurus, dark, covered. The one occurrence pairs it with darkness to intensify it — obscure darkness, a blackness beyond ordinary night — as the end of the lamp of the man who curses his parents.

Biblical Definition

The proverb is one of the severest in the book: “Whoso curseth his father or his mother, his lamp shall be put out in obscure darkness” (Proverbs 20:20). The lamp in Proverbs is the ongoing life of a house — its continuance, its name, its light in the window — and the sentence is that it goes out, and goes out into a darkness the writer has to double the words to describe. The law had made the same judgment without metaphor: “And he that curseth his father, or his mother, shall surely be put to death” (Exodus 21:17). The Lord Jesus cites that very statute against a tradition that had found a way around it: “For God commanded, saying, Honour thy father and mother: and, He that curseth father or mother, let him die the death” (Matthew 15:4). And the positive form of the commandment carries the first promise attached to any: “Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee” (Exodus 20:12). Long days for the honouring child; a lamp put out in obscure darkness for the cursing one. Scripture sets the fifth commandment at the foundation of the second table and does not treat contempt for parents as a private family matter.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines obscure as dark; destitute of light; and figuratively, not easily understood, or living in darkness.

expand to see more

OBSCURE, a. Dark; destitute of light; as the obscure night.

OBSCURITY, n. Darkness; want of light; a state of retirement from the world; a state of being unknown.

LAMP, n. A vessel with a wick, used with oil to furnish artificial light; in Scripture, a figure of life and posterity.

CURSE, v.t. To utter a wish of evil against one; to imprecate evil upon; to blaspheme.

HONOR, v.t. To revere; to respect; to treat with deference and submission, and perform relative duties to.

Key Scripture

Proverbs 20:20 — "Whoso curseth his father or his mother, his lamp shall be put out in obscure darkness."

Exodus 21:17 — "And he that curseth his father, or his mother, shall surely be put to death."

Matthew 15:4 — "For God commanded, saying, Honour thy father and mother: and, He that curseth father or mother, let him die the death."

Exodus 20:12 — "Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee."

Modern Corruption

The fifth commandment is reduced to a sentiment about family warmth, and a culture that treats contempt for parents as a stage of healthy development has no category for the proverb's severity.

expand to see more

Contempt for parents is now widely treated as a developmental phase, a necessary individuation, or the justified response of a wounded adult child. Scripture allows none of these as a general rule. The fifth commandment stands at the head of the second table, and its breach is punished in the law with death and in the Proverbs with a lamp put out in obscure darkness. The severity is not arbitrary. Parental authority is the first authority every human being meets, and a heart trained to despise it is being trained for every other rebellion, including the last one.

Scripture is not naive about bad parents. It commands fathers not to provoke their children to wrath, it records David's failures and Eli's, and it never requires obedience to a parent commanding sin. The Lord Jesus Himself, in the passage where He cites this statute, is rebuking men who used a religious device — declaring a gift Corban — to escape supporting their aged parents. That is the exact modern temptation in an older costume: finding a principled-sounding reason to withhold honour that is owed. The command survives the parent's failures because it rests on God's ordering of the family, not on the parent's merit.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ishun (H380), the blackest part of night; choshek (H2822), darkness; ner (H5216), a lamp; qalal (H7043), to curse or make light of.

expand to see more

Hebrew ishun (H380) — the pupil of the eye, hence the blackest hour; obscure darkness.

Hebrew choshek (H2822) — darkness; doubled with ishun for intensity in Proverbs 20:20.

Hebrew ner (H5216) — a lamp; in Proverbs, the life and continuance of a house.

Hebrew qalal (H7043) — to make light of, curse, treat with contempt.

Hebrew kabad (H3513) — to be heavy, to honour; the verb of the fifth commandment.

Usage

"“His lamp shall be put out in obscure darkness” — the end of the cursing child."

"“He that curseth his father, or his mother, shall surely be put to death” — the law behind it."

"“That thy days may be long upon the land” — the promise on the other side."
